It proposes three evaluation questions for compliance: whether you can produce a full audit trail for every automated decision on demand, whether the exact same criteria are applied to every candidate, documented and consistent, and whether a human makes the final call with the AI's reasoning visible to them rather than hidden in a black box. A separate post on the same page from BrightMove (857 followers) says the EU AI Act's compliance deadline for high-risk AI in employment decisions was set for 2 August 2026 and moved to December 2027, a sixteen-month extension finalised by EU lawmakers in June, while employment AI remains classified as high-risk under Annex III and the core deployer obligations around transparency, human oversight and data governance are unchanged: "The deadline moved. The underlying standard for how AI can be used in recruiting and employment decisions did not." Another post, from Lucuma Shortlist, adds that from 2 August 2026 the AI Act's transparency duties and staff AI-literacy requirements apply, while the heavier obligations for high-risk recruitment AI were pushed back to December 2027 under the recent Omnibus.

9091.gloss: Talview archives all platform videos 90 days after creation, with a 2-business-day retrieval wait
9091.verbatim: Talview's own Q4 2020 product update announcement (talview.com, Product Updates Q4-2020) states a change to its video data lifecycle: all videos on the platform created at least 90 days ago are archived. This covers Proview processed videos, Live processed videos and Async processed videos. Once archived, a video is no longer directly accessible: any retrieval request takes at least two business days, after which the user can access the video, and the retrieval must be started by raising a support ticket. This is a vendor-set lifecycle applied platform-wide, announced by Talview rather than configured by the employer.

9092.gloss: Talview's ID Verification captures images of both the candidate and their ID document, and says it keeps them encrypted
9092.verbatim: Talview's own ID Verification product page (talview.com/en/id-verification, live 2026) describes how identity data is handled. The process prompts the test-taker to present a government-issued identification document (passport, national ID card or driver's licence) in front of the webcam; the system captures images of both the test-taker and their ID document, then advanced algorithms or manual checks compare the document details against the real-time image and the information on file. On storage, the page's FAQ states that personal information and document images are encrypted and transmitted securely, that access to this data is strictly controlled, and that it is used solely for the purpose of verifying the test-taker's identity, in compliance with applicable data protection laws. The page names no retention period for those document images, and does not say whether only a match verdict is retained.

9093.gloss: Jobma states outright that it does not detect, analyze or store biometric data, and takes explicit consent before proctoring
9093.verbatim: Jobma's own Interview Fraud Prevention page (jobma.com, 2026) sets out its identity and proctoring stack and then makes three specific privacy claims under a 'Built with Privacy in Mind' heading: monitoring is non-invasive with no unnecessary interruptions; explicit candidate consent is taken before proctoring begins; and the platform 'doesn't detect, analyze, or store biometric data'. The identity layer it describes includes government ID validation, selfie verification to avoid deepfake risks, liveness detection to confirm a live candidate, and support across global identification protocols. The monitoring layer flags multiple faces on screen, copy-paste activity, window switching, mobile device usage in frame, external screen connection, and noticeable changes in the speaker's voice. Jobma also advertises downloadable interview reports, flags placed on the interview timeline, detailed candidate activity logs and 'audit-ready' structured records for compliance reviews, and its site footer carries an EU AI Act link. The page states no retention period for recordings, transcripts or proctoring evidence, and does not describe how a candidate deletion request is routed.

9094.gloss: Willo's own page claims ISO 27001 and GDPR compliance plus identity verification at screening, but publishes no retention window
9094.verbatim: Willo's own blog post '5 Spark Hire Alternatives for Faster High-Volume Screening' (willo.video, last updated 17 August 2026) describes its data and identity handling in its self-comparison. Willo says it is ISO 27001 certified and fully GDPR compliant, and that its Digital Identity Verification lets an employer verify a candidate's identity and right to work during initial screening rather than at the higher-stakes offer stage, so compliance is 'handled early on'. Alongside this it lists Real Talk, an anti-cheat feature that flags assessment responses that appear to have been completed with external help such as a script or AI assistant, plus knock-out questions and anti-cheat guardrails. Candidate material collected includes video, audio, text responses, multiple-choice answers, file uploads and CVs. Nowhere on the page does Willo state a retention period for those recordings, transcripts or identity records, whether the window is vendor-set or employer-configurable, or how a candidate deletion request is routed.

9095.gloss: Greenhouse shows what employer-configurable retention actually looks like: a day count, a timer that resets, and manual deletion
9095.verbatim: Greenhouse's own support documentation, 'Configure a data retention rule' (support.greenhouse.io, last updated 8 April 2026), sets out how an employer-configurable retention rule works in an ATS. A site admin enters the retention period in days, choosing how long candidate personal data is kept after the candidate is hired or rejected on all applications; separate rules exist for hired and rejected candidates, and rejected-candidate rules can be set per office while hired-candidate rules apply to the whole organisation and are only available to organisations using single-purpose consent. The timer starts when a candidate is hired or rejected on all applications and is applied retroactively to existing records: Greenhouse's own worked example says that if the timer is activated on 25 May 2026 with a 365-day period, the admin is emailed immediately to delete personal data for any candidate rejected on or before 25 May 2025. The timer deactivates and resets if a rejected candidate is converted into a prospect for another job, or if a job moves to an office with no rejected-candidate rule. Crucially, deletion is not automatic: 'Deleting a candidate's personal data must be done manually', and the rule only configures which named users get an email notification, on which days, at which time and time zone, telling them to do it. The admin also picks from a 'Data to be Deleted' table which fields are used to anonymise the candidate, and Greenhouse warns that deleted personal data will not show up in reports and that selecting Name and Pronunciation Recording anonymises the candidate everywhere except Activity Notes unless Activity Notes is selected too. Greenhouse advises seeking legal counsel before configuring the feature.

9096.gloss: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) is the anchor: personal data kept no longer than necessary, applicable since 25 May 2018
9096.verbatim: WorkSignal's 'Data Retention Policies: Your 2026 Guide for TA' (worksignal.com, published 1 June 2026) identifies the legal anchor for candidate-data retention as the GDPR, directly applicable from 25 May 2018, whose Article 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept 'for no longer than is necessary' for the purpose it was collected for. The piece argues that this moved retention out of housekeeping and into formal compliance, so that keeping candidate data indefinitely 'stopped looking cautious and started looking unjustified'. It draws a distinction hiring teams routinely blur: the retention policy is the governing standard (scope across ATS, scheduling tools, email, shared drives and screening vendors; roles for approvals, access reviews and deletion workflows; controls including access restrictions, encryption and logging; exceptions for litigation, audit or investigation holds; and a review cadence), while the retention schedule is the applied timeline that assigns a rule to each category such as resumes, interview notes, recordings, transcripts, offer documents or hired-candidate handoff records. It also names the operational failure mode specific to async screening: async tools generate recordings, transcripts and AI-generated summaries that pile up in separate systems, so deletion has to cover side channels (recruiter email, downloaded scorecards, spreadsheets, vendor dashboards) and not just the primary ATS, and every retention rule needs a legal hold path built before it is needed. Its practical test: if a team cannot explain the purpose and expiry logic for a candidate record, it probably should not still hold it.

9097.gloss: Recording interviews imports the candidate's home privacy regime, and about a dozen US states demand two-party consent
9097.verbatim: Writing for the National Law Review, Damon W. Silver of Jackson Lewis P.C. ('5 Key Data Privacy and Security Risks That Arise When Organizations Record Job Interviews', 13 April 2021) sets out why recording shifts the compliance burden onto the employer rather than the vendor. Privacy obligations attach to the location or residence of the data subject, not the data controller, so an organisation recording interviews of candidates residing in California or the EU may be subject to the CCPA or GDPR respectively; both require certain privacy notices, and the GDPR grants an expansive set of candidate rights over the collection, use, disclosure and retention of their data. The article notes that recordings contain far more personal information than notes or memos, because a candidate may volunteer a medical condition, religious affiliation or sexual orientation that would never reach a written record. On purpose limitation, the CCPA and GDPR require disclosure of the purposes for which personal information is used, and the GDPR may require the organisation to assess whether its purposes are overridden by the data subject's competing interests: recording to evaluate that candidate is the obvious, unobjectionable purpose, but later reuse of the same recording for staff training or marketing can trigger fresh disclosure, fresh consent and further analysis. On consent, about a dozen US states require the consent of both parties to record a conversation, so consent must be obtained from the candidate before recording begins.

9098.gloss: US floor for recruitment records: 1 year under the EEOC, 3 years under the ADEA, covering interview notes and assessments
9098.verbatim: Apollo Technical's guide 'How Long Should You Retain Employee Data?' (apollotechnical.com, by Ryan Bradshaw, 3 October 2024) sets out the US statutory minimums that sit underneath any vendor's retention setting. Under the EEOC, applications and hiring documentation must be retained for at least one year; the ADEA requires hiring and recruitment data to be kept for three years, and the guide states this explicitly includes interview notes and any assessments required during the application process. Keeping recruitment data for three years also satisfies Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and exceeds what the Americans with Disabilities Act requires. The applicant and hiring documents in scope are listed as the job posting, job application, pre-employment tests, references, background checks, offer letter, contracts and non-competes, and onboarding documentation. Beyond recruitment, the guide gives two years as best practice for personnel files, and says the ADA, ADEA and Title VII all require performance-related data to be kept for at least one year after termination, with federal contractors potentially needing two years. It also notes that non-written records fall in scope: an employer that records calls for training and monitoring may need to retain that audio too.

9099.gloss: Employment lawyer: keep pre-employment documents 3 years after the no-hire decision, and follow the longer of conflicting laws
9099.verbatim: In HR Daily Advisor's 'Ask the Expert: Recruiting Document Retention' (hrdailyadvisor.hci.org, 14 April 2020), attorney Jodi R. Bohr of Tiffany & Bosco, P.A. answers how long recruitment records should be kept for candidates who are not hired. Her answer: pre-employment documents, including job descriptions, applications and resumes, interview evaluations and offer letters, must be kept for three years after the no-hire decision is made, and generally all pre-employment documents must be retained for three years following an employee's termination. Where a candidate is hired and further documentation results, such as the Form I-9, a background check or a new hire action form, those must also be kept for three years even if the person never ends up working for the company. She stresses that state laws may impose longer periods and that where laws conflict the employer must follow the longer retention policy, giving Arizona as an example: it sets no pre-employment retention requirement, so the federal three years applies, but it requires payroll records showing daily hours, wages paid and earned sick time to be kept for four years, and the IRS suggests keeping each employee's Form W-4 for at least four years after the last tax return that used it. Statutory periods are minimums, and litigation may require keeping records longer, but where no claim is pending she advises retaining only for the minimum period.
